author: Roger Connors
title: How Do I Know If I Have Really Forgiven Someone? - Meridian Magazine
text:
One of the questions people frequently ask about forgiveness is a very practical one: “How do I know if I have really forgiven someone?”
It’s a good question. We may have prayed about an offense, told the Lord we have forgiven the person, and sincerely tried to move forward. But then we see them again, hear their name, or remember what happened—and some of those old feelings come rushing back. We wonder, If I still feel something, have I really forgiven?
In writing Healing the Wounded Heart , I wrestled with that question. I ultimately identified ten signs that can help us recognize when forgiveness is actually taking place in our hearts. They are not meant to create another standard by which we condemn ourselves. Rather, they give us a way to see whether we are moving toward the kind of forgiveness the Savior asks of us.
First, we need to understand what we are trying to accomplish. Brotherly forgiveness is a Christlike decision to obey God’s command to forgive as quickly as we are able. It means releasing those who have wronged us from blame, letting go of hurt and resentment, and trusting God to be the judge.
That definition suggests some very practical ways to determine whether we have forgiven.
Perhaps the clearest sign is that we no longer seek revenge or wish the offender harm . The desire for payback begins to disappear. We no longer need them to suffer because we suffered. That does not mean we believe there should be no consequences for wrongdoing. Justice still matters. But instead of appointing ourselves to administer justice, we trust God to do what He has promised to do.
The Lord said, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Doctrine and Covenants 82:23). Forgiveness means we are willing to let Him administer justice rather than taking that responsibility upon ourselves.
Another sign is that the emotional sting begins to soften . We may still remember what happened. We may still wish it had never occurred. But we can think about the person or the offense without experiencing the same intense anger or pain we once felt. The memory remains, but it begins losing its power over us.
We may also notice that we stop telling the story as often. When we are deeply wounded, there can be a strong desire to keep explaining what happened. We want others to understand that we were wronged. Sometimes we retell the story because we need someone to validate our pain. But as forgiveness takes hold, that need begins to diminish. We no longer need the offense to define the other person—or ourselves.
That is another important sign: we stop defining our identity by what someone did to us. Something painful may have happened to us, perhaps something profoundly unfair, but it does not have to become who we are. We move from being consumed by the wound toward living our lives again.
Perhaps an even greater indication of forgiveness is that we can begin to wish the offender well. That does not mean we want them back in our lives. Forgiveness does not always require reconciliation. We may need significant boundaries, and in some circumstances complete separation may be appropriate. But we can establish those boundaries without malice. We can hope that the person changes, heals, repents, and finds their way to Christ.
Eventually, we may even be able to pray sincerely for them.
The Savior taught, “Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). That can be extraordinarily difficult when the wound is fresh. But something powerful happens when our prayers move from Lord, make them pay to Lord, help them change; help them heal; help them come unto Thee.
Our language can reveal our progress as well. Can we speak about the person with greater neutrality or even compassion? Do we still feel a need to exaggerate their faults or emphasize our suffering? Forgiveness often shows itself not only in what we feel, but in how we speak about the person who hurt us.
And finally, there is often a growing sense of peace about the matter and the person. We feel lighter. The offender occupies less space in our minds. We are not constantly replaying the offense, imagining different outcomes, or traveling down what I call the “rabbit holes” of rumination. The burden begins to lift.
Does that mean we must experience all of these things immediately before we can say we have forgiven? I don’t think so. Forgiveness can be a process, particularly when the injury is severe. A thoughtless remark and a life-altering betrayal are not the same thing. Deep wounds may take much longer to heal.
So perhaps the best measure of forgiveness is not simply whether the hurt is gone—time, itself, has a way of making that better—but whether our heart is being filled with the love of God.
The Book of Mormon gives us this higher standard for knowing whether forgiveness is taking root in our hearts. Mormon taught that charity “suffereth long, and is kind,” “is not easily provoked,” and “thinketh no evil” (Moroni 7:45). He then identifies charity as “the pure love of Christ” and urges us to “pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love” (Moroni 7:47–48).
Perhaps, then, the ultimate evidence of forgiveness is not merely the absence of resentment , but the growing presence of charity . Can I see the person who hurt me as Christ sees them? Can I sincerely desire their welfare, their repentance, their healing, and ultimately their salvation? I may still need boundaries. I may not trust them. Reconciliation may not yet be possible. But if resentment is gradually being replaced by the pure love of Christ, that may be one of the clearest signs that forgiveness is becoming complete.
Forgiveness does not require us to forget what happened. It does not necessarily restore trust or relationships. But when we truly begin to forgive, something changes within us. The offense begins to loosen its grip. The burden becomes lighter. And increasingly, we are able to leave both the offender and the offense where they ultimately belong—in the hands of Jesus Christ.
